clips.text_en_b1: Why does everyone want to buy BTC after the move already happened? You watch BTC do nothing for weeks, ignore it completely. Then it pumps 15% and suddenly everyone wants in. Posted on /biz/ today.

signal.rationale: Post is a rant about timing, no actual setup

clips.text_en_b2: It beggars belief that people only pile into BTC once the move has already happened. BTC sat flat for weeks on end, written off completely, yet the moment it rips 15% out of nowhere, everyone suddenly wants a piece of the action. Meanwhile my prop firm position is bleeding dust and my CFD margin keeps flashing warnings, while everyone else rakes in the gains. Posted on /biz/ today, classic late entry behaviour.
clips.text_en_c1: It is genuinely bewildering how retail consistently shows up after the move has already been made. Bitcoin spent several weeks consolidating in a narrow range with virtually no engagement, and the moment it ripped 15%, the timeline flooded with anxious buyers asking whether it was too late. Classic late-stage FOMO behaviour. Over on /biz/, sentiment has flipped overnight from apathy to euphoria, while anyone running a prop firm evaluation knows the grind continues regardless of price action. My own account is grinding dust, my CFD margin is screaming warnings, and watching others catch the breakout while I nurse drawdown feels painfully familiar.
clips.text_en_c2: There is a peculiar pathology endemic to retail crypto traders, whereby capital floods in precisely when the asymmetric risk-reward has evaporated. Bitcoin idled for weeks without so much as a flicker of interest, languishing in the kind of sideways accumulation that seasoned participants recognise as coiled energy. The moment it lurched fifteen percent higher, however, the chorus of latecomers materialised en masse, compelled by the irresistible narrative that something must be done. Meanwhile, those of us leveraged through prop firm evaluations watch dust collect on barely-passing accounts, while cfd margin warnings ping with metronomic regularity, a quiet reminder that the feast, as ever, belongs to those who arrived in time and not to those who arrived at all.

clips.text_en_c1: I am seriously weighing the proposition of purchasing Cybercabs and deploying them across Tesla's robotaxi network in order to generate residual income while I focus on trading. clips.text_en_c2: I find myself increasingly preoccupied with the question of whether purchasing Cybercab units and deploying them across Tesla's nascent robotaxi network constitutes a viable, if unconventional, avenue for passive income. The proposition appeals to a particular kind of trader, one whose drawdown on a prop firm evaluation has grown wearisome and who craves, almost instinctively, a secondary revenue stream untethered from the vicissitudes of intraday volatility. Strip away the marketing veneer and what remains is a bet on autonomous utilisation rates, regulatory permissiveness, and Musk's notoriously elastic timelines. Whether this constitutes genuine financial engineering or merely a dressed-up form of hope remains, for the moment, an open question.

clips.text_en_b2: OpenAI dropped GPT-6 Astra on Thursday, boldly heralding the dawn of the AGI era, and the model reportedly comes within a hair's breadth of saturating ARC-AGI-3. The irony is not lost on me: I have barely finished my licensing exams and AI is already outpacing entry-level white-collar benchmarks. If this trajectory holds, blue-collar automation may prove far less consequential than knowledge-work displacement, and frankly, I am running out of time to adapt.
clips.text_en_c1: OpenAI formally unveiled GPT-6 Astra on Thursday, framing it as the most capable and best-aligned model they have shipped to date. Benchmarks suggest it is approaching saturation on ARC-AGI 3, a frontier that until recently seemed comfortably out of reach. The accompanying messaging essentially declared the arrival of the AGI era, and the resulting discourse across /g/ has ranged from existential dread to grudging admiration. Meanwhile, those of us still manually annotating surveys for training pipelines are confronting an uncomfortable timeline. The conventional wisdom that white-collar roles would be insulated appears increasingly optimistic.
clips.text_en_c2: OpenAI has unveiled GPT-6 Astra, a model whose performance on ARC-AGI 3 approaches saturation in a fashion that ought to give pause to anyone still optimising their curriculum vitae. The accompanying prose, suffused with the now-familiar rhetoric of welcome to the age of AGI, reads less like a product announcement than a coronation, since the underlying benchmark results are striking enough to bear the weight of the rhetoric. The implication, articulated with characteristic bluntness across /g/, is that the cognitive labour which once felt insulated from automation has acquired a disturbingly proximate expiration date, and the resentment is consequently less about the technology than about one's own timing.
